## Concrete issues

**§3.8 — `checkpoint tokens` "sliced at that session's token window"** (blocking design gap)
Claim: totals/attribution are recomputed from stored `full.jsonl` sliced at the session's token window. Code: `SessionState.TokenTranscriptStart` (`cmd/entire/cli/session/state.go:240`) is session-state only; nothing in `api/checkpoint/metadata.go` persists a token offset (only `checkpoint_transcript_start`, line 423, which `carryForwardToNewShadowBranch` resets to 0 — per commit `c69c00337`). So a reader has no window start for post-carry-forward checkpoints; slicing at `checkpoint_transcript_start` reproduces the exact cumulative bug PR A fixed. The spec needs either a persisted `token_transcript_start` in `Metadata` (PR B addition, or a PR A follow-up) or an explicit derivation (previous checkpoint's transcript length) — and legacy checkpoints can never be sliced, so attribution there must be labelled cumulative too.

**§3.1 — `flattenTokenUsage` named as existing.** No such function anywhere (`grep -rn flattenTokenUsage cmd` → none). Existing helpers are `addCheckpointTokenUsage` (`checkpoint_tokens.go:360`), `saturatingIntAdd` (`:383`), `totalTokens` (`status_style.go:111`). §7 lists it ambiguously; mark it new.

**§3.1/§7 — `addCheckpointTokenUsage` drops PR A's fields.** `checkpoint_tokens.go:360-380` copies `Input/CacheCreation/CacheRead/Output/APICallCount` field-by-field and silently loses `ThinkingTokens`, `CacheCreation1hTokens`, `Model`. The spec says the flattening "stays in `cli` with the existing saturating helpers" — as written they would zero the subset fields the whole design depends on. CLAUDE.md explicitly calls this pattern out ("a field-by-field copy is how the nested total came to be dropped") and names `types.AddTokenUsage` as the single summing primitive. The spec should say the flatten helper is rewritten on `AddTokenUsage` (or extended and tested for the three new fields).

**§7 — `cmd/entire/cli/tokens_cmd.go` does not exist.** The `tokens` group is `newTokensGroupCmd()` in `tokens_profile.go:52` (`Hidden: true`, RunE → `cmd.Help()`); `session tokens` is `newTokensCmd()` in `session_tokens.go:80`, registered from `sessions.go:194`.

**§4 / §3.6 — the worked example contradicts the threshold table.** Example recommendation: "Context growth was the largest cost (41%)". §3.6 Claude `context-growth` threshold is ≥ 55% of cost. On the spec's own numbers this rule would not fire; the example needs a different rule (or the threshold text needs the "largest class" alternative trigger spelled out).

**§4 — `formatTokenCount` cannot render "3.7M" / "4.1M".** `status_style.go:99-109` only emits `k` (3,700,000 → `"3700k"`); the parity table in `status_test.go:862` pins that. Either add an M tier (and update the parity table, so it is not a pure move) or change the example.

**§1 item 4 — "Cache read is 94–96% of volume on every agent … 51–54% of cost".** Grounding §6: Gemini cache-read is 58% of volume / 24% of cost (median). True for Claude/Codex/OpenCode/Pi only.

**§1 item 3 — "Gemini double-counted cache (+58–89%)".** Sources say +58% (commit `51f130261`, one real checkpoint) and +70% (grounding §2). The 89% figure appears in neither.

**§1 item 5 / §3.4 — "Cursor records nothing".** True for the 38 legacy checkpoints, but `agent/cursor/lifecycle.go:134` (`tokenUsageFromStop`) captures input/cache_read/cache_write/output per turn from the stop hook, and CLAUDE.md says "Cursor tokens come only from stop-hook payloads". The Cursor profile row should allow the Usage table from `state.TokenUsage`/metadata (no thinking, no TTL, no tools) rather than "not recorded" wholesale; the mock doc already hints at this ("predates Cursor's per-turn token fields").

**Header / §3.10 — "all experimental / `entire labs`".** `checkpoint tokens` (`checkpoint_group.go:42`) and `session tokens` (`sessions.go:194`) use plain `AddCommand`, no `Hidden`, no `experimental.Register` — they are canonical visible group verbs per CLAUDE.md ("`checkpoint`: `list`, `explain`, `tokens`, `search`"). Only the `tokens` group is experimental. The "Breaking: recommendation IDs change (labs-only)" caveat is therefore not accurate for the two visible commands.

**§3.5 — "required method on all five stores".** Six production `ReadSessionContent` implementers: `persistent.go:1484`, `refs_store.go`, `routing_store.go`, `fanout.go:50`, `fsstore/fsstore.go`, `checkpoint_api_reader.go:272`. §7 lists all six; the count in §3.5 (and the 08-25 §3.6 it cites) is off by one. Seven test fakes: confirmed.

**§3.6 `cache-miss` row — "p90 49%" is Codex-only.** Grounding: OpenCode fresh-input p90 = 39%, so a shared ≥ 45% threshold sits above OpenCode's p90 while the row cites Codex's. State both or split.

**§3.3 — Gemini "session-level" model.** `geminicli/transcript.go:180-182` says real Gemini message rows carry a `model` field ("timestamp, model, and tokens that are present in real Gemini transcripts"). Worth re-checking a transcript before locking Gemini to session-level weighting.

## Sections that check out
- §3.1: `types.TokenUsage` has `ThinkingTokens`, `CacheCreation1hTokens`, `Model` (`agent/types/token_usage.go:24-36`); `AddTokenUsage`/`SubtractTokenUsage` propagate them.
- `api/checkpoint.CheckpointSummary.TokenUsageVersion` + `const TokenUsageVersionDelta = 2` (`metadata.go:594-599`), stamped in `persistent.go:822` and `fsstore.go:147`; the legacy-signal description in §3.7 matches the field's doc comment exactly; "before v0.11" is consistent with CHANGELOG top = 0.10.2.
- §3.8 symbols: `SessionReader.ReadSessionContent(ctx, id, sessionIndex) (*SessionContent, error)` with `.Transcript []byte` (`interfaces.go:20`, `metadata.go:369`); `strategy.ResolveTranscriptPath(state *SessionState) (string, error)` (`strategy/resolve_transcript.go:17`); `paths.SubagentsDir(transcriptDir, sessionID)` (`paths.go:259`, sessionID = the agent's ID). Current loading: `session tokens` → `strategy.LoadSessionState` + `state.TokenUsage` only (Source `"session_state"`); `checkpoint tokens` → `store.Read` + `ReadSessionMetadata` per session, root `summary.TokenUsage` fallback (Source `"committed_checkpoint"`); `profile` → same metadata path via `checkpointTokenUsage`, `--limit 50`/`--all`. No transcript reads today.
- §3.5 new items are genuinely new: no `tokenreport/`, no `token_attribution.go`, no `TokenAttributor`/`AsTokenAttributor` (`capabilities.go` has the `AsTokenCalculator` pattern at :141), no `api/checkpoint.TaskRecord`/`ReadTaskRecords` (only `session.TaskRecord`, `state.go:457`). `tasks/<id>/task.json` layout and `taskRecordMetadata` fields (`persistent.go:469-531, 1310`) match; `FetchingTree.RawEntries`, `getCheckpointFetchingTree`, `checkpointTree`, `readOrder`/`firstResolved` all exist. `SkillEventTranscriptAnchor{Unit,Start,End,EntryIDs,ToolUseID}` (`skill_events.go:54`) matches.
- §3.4/§3.5 parser facts: Codex reads only cumulative `total_token_usage`, subtracts `cached_input_tokens`, keeps `reasoning_output_tokens` (`codex/transcript.go:270-335`); OpenCode `Tokens.BilledOutput()` uses the total identity, `Part.Type/Tool` (`opencode/types.go:69-107`); Gemini `tokens.{cached,thoughts,tool}` + `toolCalls` (`geminicli/types.go:97-103`, `transcript.go:28`); Pi `Usage.CacheWrite1h`, `Message.Model`, `toolCall` parts (`pijsonl.go:80-99`, `pi/transcript.go:107`); Claude `thinking_tokens`, `ephemeral_5m/1h`, `message.model`, `tool_use` (`claudecode/types.go:113-127`). Neither Codex `turn_context.*`, Claude `effort`/`attributionSkill`, OpenCode `modelID`, nor Pi `cost`/`thinking_level_change` is parsed today — consistent with the spec treating them as new reads.
- §3.6 vs grounding §6: Claude context-replay ≥70 (p90 71), Codex ≥67 (p90 67), Pi ≥66 (p90 66), Pi context-growth ≥45 (p90 45), model-choice fire rates 2/6/17%, Codex effort median 36–40 / p90 52, "cache write largest in 37%" (123/332) all match. §1's 64%/65% rule fire rates trace to the 08-25 spec §3.10 table; the 53%/4.03B claim traces to commit `c69c00337`. Current `context-pressure` constant is 80 (`session_tokens.go:73`).
- §4 numbers match the mock doc (rows, totals, 57% thinking-of-output, 3-item remainder = 16.2k+11.2k); only cosmetic diffs (skill label abbreviated, 5-min row dropped).
- §3.9: `AgentTypeVogon = "Vogon Agent"` (`vogon.go:27`); "Mock Lifecycle Agent" is the `lifecycle_test.go:100` fixture string.
- CLAUDE.md: plain text + `--json`, no TTY gating, and `types.AddTokenUsage` as the sole summing primitive are respected apart from the flatten-helper issue above; no `gitrepo`/`Status` concerns arise since the commands read stores and session state.

## Advisory
- Codex `APICallCount` counts every `token_count` event including the 10–13% duplicates (`codex/transcript.go:298`), so "N API calls" and the "≥ 20 calls" gate are inflated on Codex; the dedupe the spec mandates for deltas should also feed the call count.
- `formatPercent` already exists (`session_tokens.go:407`); §3.1's `FormatPercent` should be noted as a move, like `FormatTokenCount`.
- `--compare` JSON today is `{baseline,current,change,change_percent,direction}` (`checkpoint_tokens.go:50`); mirror that shape for `cost_share` rather than a bare `{baseline,current}`.
- Once `checkpoint tokens` reads transcripts it needs a `SessionReader`, not the narrower `reviewContextSessionMetadataReader` it takes now (`checkpoint_tokens.go:162`); worth a line in §7.
- §3.4 claims Codex "✓ thinking" but Claude Code "since Aug 2026" — the Codex row could carry a similar "since" qualifier if `reasoning_output_tokens` was ever absent; not verified either way.</result>

content.text:
While the suites run for the follow-up commit, here's what the spec review turned up and what I did with it.

## The one real gap (fixed in PR A, pending push)
PR A persisted the token window in *session state* but not in the checkpoint's metadata — so `checkpoint tokens` would have had no way to slice the stored `full.jsonl` to the token window, and slicing at `checkpoint_transcript_start` would re-create the cumulative bug. Added `token_transcript_start` to session `metadata.json` (WriteOptions → Metadata → both stores → strategy), test-first (RED `0, want 2` → GREEN), lint clean, affected packages green. Full suites running now; I'll push it onto PR #2155 when they pass.

## Spec corrections applied (`2026-08-28-…-breakdown-first-design.md`)
- `flattenTokenUsage` is **new**, not existing, and must be built on `types.AddTokenUsage` — the current `addCheckpointTokenUsage` copies five fields by hand and would silently zero `thinking_tokens`/`cache_creation_1h_tokens`. Exactly the trap CLAUDE.md warns about; good catch.
- `formatTokenCount` has no `M` tier today (prints `3700k`) — spec now says add it and update the parity table.
- Gemini records `model` **per message** (verified on the real transcripts) → per-call weighting, not session-level.
- Cursor isn't "records nothing": its stop hook gives per-turn totals, so it gets a usage row — just no breakdown/thinking/TTL.
- `checkpoint tokens` and `session tokens` are **visible canonical verbs**, not labs-only — so the recommendation-ID change is a documented `--json` break on visible commands. Added as **§8.5 for your decision** (accept, or alias old IDs for a release).
- Worked example contradicted the table (cache write 41% < Claude's 55% threshold): example now fires `effort` (thinking 57% of output) instead.
- Six store implementers, not five; `cache-miss` thresholds split Codex 45% / OpenCode 40%; Codex API-call count must dedupe duplicate events; `--compare` JSON mirrors the existing shape; `checkpoint tokens` needs the wider `SessionReader`; file table points at `tokens_profile.go`'s `newTokensGroupCmd`, not a nonexistent `tokens_cmd.go`; Gemini's volume/cost figures excluded from the "every agent" claim; +58–89% cited to the verifier run.

Everything else — the PR A fields, `TokenUsageVersion`, `ReadSessionContent`/`ResolveTranscriptPath`/`SubagentsDir` shapes, the per-agent parser facts, the §3.6 numbers against the calibration, the §4 numbers against the mock-ups — checked out.

The spec is ready for you to read:
```
less docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-28-token-reports-breakdown-first-design.md
```
§8 now has five inputs to settle before code: OpenAI/Google ratios, Pi dollars, bare `entire tokens`, per-agent thresholds after the calibration re-run, and the ID-break handling.

1. **One command shown** — §4 only rendered `checkpoint tokens`; it should show all three (plus bare `entire tokens`), since `session tokens` is forward-looking and `profile` is a different shape entirely.
2. **Not actionable** — "lower effort for routine steps" names a direction, not an action. An actionable line needs: the exact lever for *that* agent (setting/command), what's at stake in tokens/cost, and how to check it worked. 3. **Visual aid** — a proportional bar column in the tables is cheap and terminal-safe; richer visuals belong to the web follow-up.

Spec updated (same path). What changed:

## Actionability contract (§3.6)
A recommendation prints **only if all four parts can be filled from data**; otherwise the rule stays silent and the breakdown speaks for itself:

| part | example |
|---|---|
| **Evidence** | "164.6k tokens (32% of cost) were Bash output read into context under systematic-debugging — 11 of its 14 Bash calls returned >10k tokens" |
| **Action** | one exact thing to do in *this* agent: "Pipe those through `head`/`grep`, or ask for the specific lines" / "Set `model_reasoning_effort` to medium in `~/.codex/config.toml`" — never "consider", "reduce", "be mindful" |
| **Stake** | a ceiling derived from the breakdown, not a forecast: "at most the 32% this contributor represents" |
| **Check** | how to see it worked: `entire session tokens` after the next turn, or `entire checkpoint tokens <next> --compare <this>` |

Plus a per-agent **lever table** — the exact strings the copy is allowed to use. I've marked it as *working assumptions that must be verified against each agent's docs* before code (new §8.5). If a lever can't be verified for an agent, that rule is ineligible there and Notes says so. That's the honest version of "actionable": no lever, no advice.

## All three commands rendered (§4)
- **4.1 `checkpoint tokens`** — retrospective; the example now carries two contract-conforming recommendations (Bash output size → `head`/`grep`; thinking 57% at `high` → effort medium), each with stake + check. Cache write is the largest class (41%) but under Claude's 55% threshold, so no third line — the table already shows it.
- **4.2 `session tokens`** — same tables, forward-looking voice ("so far", "for the remaining searches"), check = next turn. Example: "Subagent: Explore used 4.7M tokens across 5 dispatches, all on claude-fable-5 → set `model: haiku` on the Explore agent definition." `--agent-brief`'s next-best-action line becomes the **Action** part verbatim, so the agent gets the same concrete instruction the human does.

Numbers are the calibration sample's arranged in the proposed shape, labelled as such.
- **4.4 bare `entire tokens`** — runs 4.2; no session → one-line hint, exit 0.

## Visual aid (§3.11)
A proportional **bar column** in every table — `▇▇▇▇▁▁▁▁▁▁▁▁`, 12 cells, ASCII fallback when stdout isn't UTF-8 — like `git --stat`'s histogram. Omitted from `--json`/`--agent-brief`. content.text:
Agreed on all three counts, and the fix was structural, not wording. Here's what changed in the spec.

## Recommendations → "Fixes"
The evidence/stake/check scaffold is gone. A recommendation is now one line, and it exists only when it can name a **specific target** and a **specific edit**:

```
Fixes
  Add `-run <TestName>` or `| tail -30` to `go test ./cmd/entire/...` — 9 calls, 140.2k tokens read back (27%).
  Set effort to medium for this kind of debugging — thinking was 65.3k of 115.1k output tokens (57%).
```

Sources of fixes, each requiring something concrete to point at: a **command pattern** that dominates Bash output; a **file** read whole repeatedly or oversized; a **skill** loaded more than once; a **subagent type** on the parent's premium model ("add `model: haiku` to `.claude/agents/explore.md`"); the **effort setting** when thinking ≥ 50% *and* the agent's selector is verified; `/compact` in a live session when the same context has been replayed ≥ 20 times; trimmed tool output on OpenAI-provider agents when fresh input dominates. Cap 2, gate ≥ 10% of cost, and **nothing printed when nothing is nameable** — no "looks fine". Every class-share rule from the old spec (`context-growth`, `model-choice`, `context-pressure`…) is dropped: those sentences described the table.

## Attribution goes one level deeper
To make fixes nameable, the breakdown gets a drill-down under each top contributor — the command's leading words, the file path, the host, the skill + invocation count, the subagent type + model:

```
  Bash (under systematic-debugging)    164.6k    32%
    go test ./cmd/entire/...  9 calls  140.2k
    git log -p                2 calls   18.1k
    grep -rn                  3 calls    6.3k
```
That row is what turns "Bash was 32%" into "`go test ./cmd/entire/...` × 9".

## `profile` prints no recommendations
It's an aggregate; a fix has to point at something. It now lists **"worth opening"** — the top-cost checkpoints per agent with the one figure that stands out — and points at `entire checkpoint tokens <id>`.

## Bars removed
§3.11 now says: no glyphs in the terminal; visuals are the web's job, and the JSON (now including the drill-down details) carries what it needs.

`--json`: `recommendations[]` is replaced by `fixes[]{target, edit, tokens, share}` — a documented break on the two visible commands (§8.6).

Same path, §3.6 and §4:
```
less ~/dev/entire/devenv/entireio/cli/.worktrees/tokens/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-28-token-reports-breakdown-first-design.md
```

One honest caveat on the effort fix: it's only as actionable as the selector name we print, and I haven't verified Claude Code's (or Pi's) current one. Until that's confirmed against the docs (§8.5), the spec says that line is not printed at all.

this is better, still kind of hard for the viewer to follow. Mostly because reader can't see the 27% in the output, because the systematic debugging was separated and the 27% wasn't listed there but only in the recommendations whihc is now fixes, I still think this change is confusing, like recommendations is clearer I think. And to me this also doesn't make sense. 

When I read this, this doesn't read like a sentence, and is this too niche in general? And we also would want to know how long the session was, that's important, like for this session, if it was 10 hours, is this something we want our agent to remember for future sessions? can we generalize somehow? like store in agent memroy? 

Do you see what I'm trying to get at?

Yes. Three things, and they point in one direction.

**1. The numbers have to line up.** A reader shouldn't meet "27%" for the first time in a recommendation. If the table says Bash 32% and the sub-row says `go test` 140.2k with no share, the recommendation can't cite 27%. Every number a recommendation uses must be a number visible in a table row — same grouping, same label, same figure. And I split one thing into two rows ("Bash under systematic-debugging" and "Skill: systematic-debugging") which makes the reader reassemble it. One grouping.

**2. "Fixes" was the wrong move, and so was the telegraphic format.** Keep the name **Recommendations**, write sentences. My mistake was equating "actionable" with "micro-specific": `add -run <TestName> to go test ./cmd/entire/...` is actionable for exactly one session and reads like a lint warning. You're asking whether that's even the right altitude — and it isn't, on its own.

**3. The real point: a recommendation is worth something when it generalizes — and then it should be *remembered*, not printed.** A 10-hour session that replays the same context 70 times isn't a "run /compact" tip; it's "long sessions cost you N× — start a new session per task", and that's a habit, not a fix. "Explore ran on Opus 5 times" becomes valuable when the profile shows it's happened in 30 of your last 50 sessions — and at that point the right output isn't a line on a report, it's a line in the agent's memory or instructions so it *does it* next time. That's your original step 3 ("then optimize"), the customer's `token optimize` ask, and "eventually part of the brain" — the unit of value is a durable, generalized instruction the agent acts on, and the per-session report is where you *discover* it.

So the layer above the breakdown looks like this:

- **Header gets duration** — `Duration: 9h 42m · 43 API calls · 4.1M tokens`. Wall-clock is the dimension that explains replay and cache-TTL cost, and "tokens per hour" is what makes sessions comparable. It's in every transcript (timestamps) and cheap.
- **Recommendations (≤ 2, sentences)** come in two kinds, and the report says which:
  - *This session:* an observation with a plain-language cause — "Most of this session's cost was re-reading its own context: 43 turns over 9 hours replayed ~90k tokens each time. Splitting work like this into shorter sessions is the single biggest lever."
  - *Pattern:* something the profile has seen recur — "Explore subagents ran on your main model in 31 of your last 50 sessions (≈ 18% of spend). Running them on Haiku is a one-line change in the agent definition."
- **Remembering:** a pattern recommendation can be saved with one command — `entire tokens remember <n>` — which writes an approved, general instruction into the agent's own memory/instruction file (Claude Code memory dir or `CLAUDE.md`, Codex `AGENTS.md`, etc.), e.g. *"Run Explore/search subagents on haiku."* / *"Pipe verbose test output through tail."* Human-approved, per repo, and the agent enforces it every session. That's how a niche observation becomes general without us guessing — recurrence promotes it, the user confirms it, the agent remembers it. It also gives the "after 3 sessions, Entire notices" idea a concrete form without doing any magic behind the user's back.

If that's the direction you mean, the spec changes are: duration in the header and as a profile dimension; one consistent grouping with every cited number visible; recommendations renamed back, in sentences, two kinds with the pattern kind sourced from the profile's recurrence; and a small `remember` surface writing to agent memory. do you think adding more commands is right? or how else can we tell user the best way to update agent memory or do it for them with existing infra with these commands?

No — I don't think a new command is right, and Entire already has the pieces to do this without one.

**What exists**

- `session tokens --agent-brief` / `checkpoint tokens --agent-brief` — an *agent-directed* output the agent is meant to read mid-session. It's the natural carrier for a pattern.
- Every agent already manages its own durable instructions/memory: Claude Code's auto-memory (`~/.claude/projects/<repo>/memory/`) and `CLAUDE.md`, Codex/OpenCode `AGENTS.md`, Gemini `GEMINI.md` + `/memory add`, Cursor rules. The agent knows how to write to it; the user already approves such writes in conversation.
- `agent-help` and the `entire:` skill plugin tell agents *when* to run a command and what to do with the result — that's exactly where "how to use token findings" belongs per CLAUDE.md's own table (guidance goes in `agentHelpGuidance`, never in a `Long`).

**How it fits together, zero new surface**

1. The brief gains a `Pattern:` block when the profile has a recurring one — e.g. *"Explore subagents ran on the main model in 31 of your last 50 sessions (≈18% of spend). If the user agrees, remember: run Explore/search subagents on a smaller model."* Written as an instruction the agent can store verbatim.
2. `agent-help` guidance for `session tokens` says: run `--agent-brief` when the user asks about cost or after a long session; if it contains a `Pattern`, propose it to the user and, on yes, save it to your memory/instructions file. The `entire:` skill carries the same steps for Claude Code.
3. The human report ends with the same pattern sentence in a copy-pasteable form — for someone who'd rather paste it into `CLAUDE.md` themselves.

The user approves in chat, the agent writes it where it already keeps such things, and from then on the agent enforces it. Entire discovers the pattern; it doesn't write into anyone's memory behind their back — which is also why I wouldn't have a hook do it.

**Where a command *would* be justified, and why not yet**

A `remember` command is deterministic and agent-agnostic (writes the right file for each agent without trusting the agent to do it). It's worth adding if the brief route proves unreliable — agents ignoring the pattern, or no-channel agents (Cursor, Copilot) that never run the brief. Until we see that, it's speculative surface, and CLAUDE.md's bar for new agent-facing commands is high for good reason.

**One thing to keep straight**

The pattern's source is the **profile** (recurrence across sessions), not the single session — a one-off `go test` observation should never be offered as a memory. That keeps "too niche" out by construction: only things that recurred get proposed.

So in the spec: no `remember` command; `--agent-brief` gains the pattern block sourced from the profile; `agentHelpGuidance` + the skill carry the propose-and-save steps; the human report prints the pattern sentence. Want me to fold that in with the §3.6/§4 rewrite (duration, one grouping, sentences, two kinds of recommendation)?

content.text:
Added as §3.11 "Automation — the pattern nudge". It rides entirely on hooks Entire already runs.

## What happens, end to end, with nobody asking

1. **Every turn end** (existing Stop hook): Entire computes this session's causes from what the hook already has in session state — totals, duration, subagent model — and appends them to a small local ledger, `.git/entire-token-patterns.json` (per user, never committed). No transcript re-read; microseconds.
2. **Promotion:** a cause that has fired in ≥ 40% of your last 50 sessions for that agent becomes a pattern — the ledger is just the profile kept incrementally.
3. **Next session start** (existing context injection, channel agents): if a pattern is `new`, one line goes in — *"Entire found a recurring token pattern for this repo; run `entire session tokens --agent-brief` and propose its memory line to the user."* The agent runs it, gets the `Memory:` line, and asks you.
4. **You answer once.** Yes → the agent writes its memory (§3.6) and records the outcome with `entire session tokens --pattern-accepted subagent_model` (a flag, not a command); no → `--pattern-declined`. The ledger never nudges that pattern again. A pattern left unanswered backs off for 10 sessions.
5. **Skip even the question:** `tokens.auto_remember: true` in `.entire/settings.local.json` (local layer only — it's a personal preference) tells the agent via the brief to save the memory line without asking. Default off. Entire itself still never writes a memory file.
6. **Cursor / Copilot / humans:** `entire status` shows *"1 token pattern to review — entire tokens"* while one is `new`, with the `remember:` line to paste.

Net effect: after ~20 sessions with the same habit, the agent brings it up once, unprompted, with a one-word approval — then it's in memory and it stops.

## What this changes in the decisions list (§8)
- **§8.9** — the session-start line is the one exception to CLAUDE.md's "first-turn injection carries only invariants". It's gated on a durable repo-level fact, is ≤ 1 line, and self-silences; I think that meets the bar, but it's the rule you set, so it's flagged. Alternative: restrict the nudge to `entire status` + the brief and accept lower pickup.
- **§8.10** — keep or drop the `auto_remember` opt-in.
- The hook-side nudge moves out of "deferred" — it was deferred earlier because it was premature before the breakdown existed; it isn't anymore.

Yes — for the human path that's simpler and better than anything in §3.11, and it removes most of the machinery. Two things need care.

**1. Who writes the file.** If Entire itself writes on your "y", it has to know where. Writing into Claude Code's *personal* memory dir (frontmatter format, per-user path) is fragile and agent-specific. The clean target is the **repo instruction file the enabled agents already read** — `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` / `GEMINI.md` (in this repo `AGENTS.md` is a symlink to `CLAUDE.md`). Entire knows which agents are enabled, so it knows which file(s); it appends under a `## Token habits` heading, idempotently. That's shared, versioned, reviewed in a PR like any instruction — and it's the same kind of write `entire enable` already does to agent config. Personal memory stays the *agent's* job on the brief path.

**2. Agents can't answer a prompt.** The report must not be TTY-gated for the information (CLAUDE.md's agent-safe rule), so: the confirm shows only when stdout is a TTY (`NewAccessibleForm`), and `--remember <cause>` / `--dismiss <cause>` are the non-interactive equivalents — which also replace the clunkier `--pattern-accepted/declined` flags I had. The `remember:` line prints in the output regardless, so a non-TTY caller still sees exactly what would be written.

So the layer simplifies to:

- **Human runs any of the three commands** → report ends with:
  ```
  Remember for your agents? Appends to CLAUDE.md under "## Token habits":
    "Run Explore/search subagents on a smaller model."
  [y/N]
  ```
  y → Entire appends, records `accepted` in the ledger. N → `declined`, never asked again.
- **Agent runs the brief** → unchanged: it proposes in chat, writes its own memory on yes, records with `--remember`.
- **Automatic surfacing** → the turn-end ledger and the single session-start line stay; they're what makes the agent bring it up unprompted. Without them, "automatic" would mean "whenever you happen to run the command".
- `auto_remember` opt-in → drop it. The prompt is one keystroke; the agent path already asks in chat.

Folding that into §3.11 now.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/peytonmontei/.claude/plugins/cache/superpowers-marketplace/superpowers/5.0.2/skills/writing-plans

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** This should be run in a dedicated worktree (created by brainstorming skill).

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (if subagents available) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## Remember
- Exact file paths always
- Complete code in plan (not "add validation")
- Exact commands with expected output
- Reference relevant skills with @ syntax
- DRY, YAGNI, TDD, frequent commits

## Plan Review Loop

After completing each chunk of the plan:

1. Dispatch plan-document-reviewer subagent (see plan-document-reviewer-prompt.md) with precisely crafted review context — never your session history. This keeps the reviewer focused on the plan, not your thought process.
   - Provide: chunk content, path to spec document
2. If ❌ Issues Found:
   - Fix the issues in the chunk
   - Re-dispatch reviewer for that chunk
   - Repeat until ✅ Approved
3. If ✅ Approved: proceed to next chunk (or execution handoff if last chunk)

**Chunk boundaries:** Use `## Chunk N: <name>` headings to delimit chunks. Each chunk should be ≤1000 lines and logically self-contained.

**Review loop guidance:**
- Same agent that wrote the plan fixes it (preserves context)
- If loop exceeds 5 iterations, surface to human for guidance
- Reviewers are advisory - explain disagreements if you believe feedback is incorrect

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Ready to execute?"**

**Execution path depends on harness capabilities:**

**If harness has subagents (Claude Code, etc.):**
- **REQUIRED:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Do NOT offer a choice - subagent-driven is the standard approach
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If harness does NOT have subagents:**
- Execute plan in current session using superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

| **Discounts**       | Applied as fewer CCUs metered                                                                                                                                                                                     |

One hundred (100) CCU represents $1.00 USD of fees owed for the Services, calculated at the applicable prices on [claude.com/pricing#api](https://claude.com/pricing#api), after application of any discounts.
</Note>

### Inference geography

See [Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency) for details.

## Feature-specific pricing

### Prompt caching

Prompt caching reduces costs and latency by reusing previously processed portions of your prompt across API calls. Instead of reprocessing the same large system prompt, document, or conversation history on every request, the API reads from cache at a fraction of the standard input price.

There are two ways to enable prompt caching:

* **Automatic caching:** Add a single `cache_control` field at the top level of your request. The system automatically manages cache breakpoints as conversations grow. This is the recommended starting point for most use cases.
* **Explicit cache breakpoints:** Place `cache_control` directly on individual content blocks for fine-grained control over exactly what gets cached.

Prompt caching uses the following pricing multipliers relative to base input token rates:

| Cache operation      | Multiplier             | Duration                             |
| -------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| 5-minute cache write | 1.25x base input price | Cache valid for 5 minutes            |
| 1-hour cache write   | 2x base input price    | Cache valid for 1 hour               |
| Cache read (hit)     | 0.1x base input price  | Same duration as the preceding write |

Cache write tokens are charged when content is first stored. Cache read tokens are charged when a subsequent request retrieves the cached content. A cache hit costs 10% of the standard input price, which means caching pays off after one cache read for the 5-minute duration (1.25x write), or after two cache reads for the 1-hour duration (2x write).

These multipliers stack with other pricing modifiers, including the Batch API discount and data residency.

For implementation details, supported models, and code examples, see [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching).

### Data residency pricing

For Claude 4.6 and later models, specifying US-only inference through the `inference_geo` parameter incurs a 1.1x multiplier on all token pricing categories, including input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads. Global routing (the default) uses standard pricing.

This applies to the Claude API (first-party) and Claude Platform on AWS. On Claude in Microsoft Foundry, the same 1.1x multiplier applies to deployments that use the US Data Zone Standard deployment type (see [Inference geography](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#foundry-inference-geography)). Partner-operated platforms (Bedrock and Google Cloud) have independent regional pricing. See [Bedrock](https://aws.amazon.com/bedrock/pricing/) and [Google Cloud](https://cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/pricing#claude-models) for details. Earlier models do not support the `inference_geo` parameter and always use standard pricing; requests that include the parameter on these models return a 400 error.

For more information, see [Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency).

### Fast mode pricing

[Fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode), in research preview, provides significantly faster output for Claude Opus 5 and Claude Opus 4.8 at premium pricing. Fast mode pricing applies across the full context window, including requests over 200k input tokens. Fast mode is available on the Claude API (first-party) only; it is not available on Claude Platform on AWS or partner-operated cloud platforms.

| Model                           | Input      | Output     |
| ------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------- |
| Claude Opus 5 / Claude Opus 4.8 | $10 / MTok | $50 / MTok |

Fast mode is not available on Claude Opus 4.7 (requests with `speed: "fast"` return an error) or Claude Opus 4.6 (requests run at standard speed and are billed at standard rates). See [Fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode#supported-models).

Fast mode pricing stacks with other pricing modifiers:

* [Prompt caching multipliers](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#prompt-caching) apply on top of fast mode pricing
* [Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency) multipliers apply on top of fast mode pricing

Fast mode is not available with the [Batch API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#batch-processing).

For more information, see [Fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode).

### Batch processing

The Batch API allows asynchronous processing of large volumes of requests with a 50% discount on both input and output tokens.

| Model                                                                                                                                 | Batch input  | Batch output  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------- |
| Claude Fable 5                                                                                                                        | $5 / MTok    | $25 / MTok    |
| Claude Mythos 5 ([limited availability](https://anthropic.com/glasswing))                                                             | $5 / MTok    | $25 / MTok    |
| Claude Opus 5                                                                                                                         | $2.50 / MTok | $12.50 / MTok |
| Claude Opus 4.8                                                                                                                       | $2.50 / MTok | $12.50 / MTok |
| Claude Opus 4.7                                                                                                                       | $2.50 / MTok | $12.50 / MTok |
| Claude Opus 4.6                                                                                                                       | $2.50 / MTok | $12.50 / MTok |
| Claude Opus 4.5                                                                                                                       | $2.50 / MTok | $12.50 / MTok |
| Claude Opus 4.1 ([retired, except on Bedrock and Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations))  | $7.50 / MTok | $37.50 / MTok |
| Claude Opus 4 ([retired, except on Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations))                | $7.50 / MTok | $37.50 / MTok |
| Claude Sonnet 5                                                                                                                       | $1 / MTok    | $5 / MTok     |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6                                                                                                                     | $1.50 / MTok | $7.50 / MTok  |
| Claude Sonnet 4.5                                                                                                                     | $1.50 / MTok | $7.50 / MTok  |
| Claude Sonnet 4 ([retired, except on Bedrock and Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations))  | $1.50 / MTok | $7.50 / MTok  |
| Claude Haiku 4.5                                                                                                                      | $0.50 / MTok | $2.50 / MTok  |
| Claude Haiku 3.5 ([retired, except on Bedrock and Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)) | $0.40 / MTok | $2 / MTok     |

For more information about batch processing, see [Batch processing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/batch-processing).

### Long context pricing

Claude 4.6 and later models and [Claude Mythos Preview](https://anthropic.com/glasswing) include the full [1M token context window](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows) at standard pricing. (A 900k-token request is billed at the same per-token rate as a 9k-token request.) Prompt caching and batch processing discounts apply at standard rates across the full context window.

### Tool use pricing

Tool use requests are priced based on:

1. The total number of input tokens sent to the model (including in the `tools` parameter)
2. The number of output tokens generated
3. For server-side tools, additional usage-based pricing (for example, web search charges per search performed)

Client-side tools are priced the same as any other Claude API request, although server-side tools can incur additional charges based on their specific usage.

The additional tokens from tool use come from:

* The `tools` parameter in API requests (tool names, descriptions, and schemas)
* `tool_use` content blocks in API requests and responses
* `tool_result` content blocks in API requests

When you use `tools`, the API also automatically includes a special system prompt for the model that enables tool use. The number of tool use tokens required for each model is listed in the following table (excluding the additional tokens listed earlier). Note that the table assumes at least 1 tool is provided. If no `tools` are provided, then a tool choice of `none` uses 0 additional system prompt tokens.

| Model                                                                                                                                 | Tool choice                    | Tool use system prompt token count |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| Claude Opus 5                                                                                                                         | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 286 tokens***406 tokens            |
| Claude Opus 4.8                                                                                                                       | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 290 tokens***410 tokens            |
| Claude Opus 4.7                                                                                                                       | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 675 tokens***804 tokens            |
| Claude Opus 4.6                                                                                                                       | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 497 tokens***589 tokens            |
| Claude Opus 4.5                                                                                                                       | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 496 tokens***588 tokens            |
| Claude Opus 4.1 ([retired, except on Bedrock and Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations))  | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 313 tokens***315 tokens            |
| Claude Opus 4 ([retired, except on Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations))                | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 313 tokens***315 tokens            |
| Claude Sonnet 5                                                                                                                       | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 354 tokens***474 tokens            |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6                                                                                                                     | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 497 tokens***589 tokens            |
| Claude Sonnet 4.5                                                                                                                     | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 496 tokens***588 tokens            |
| Claude Sonnet 4 ([retired, except on Bedrock and Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations))  | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 313 tokens***315 tokens            |
| Claude Haiku 4.5                                                                                                                      | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 496 tokens***588 tokens            |
| Claude Haiku 3.5 ([retired, except on Bedrock and Google Cloud](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)) | `auto`, `none`***`any`, `tool` | 264 tokens***355 tokens            |

These token counts are added to your normal input and output tokens to calculate the total cost of a request.

For current per-model prices, refer to the [model pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#model-pricing) section.

For more information about tool use implementation and best practices, see [Tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview).

### Specific tool pricing

#### Bash tool

The bash tool definition adds the following input tokens to your request. This is in addition to the per-model [tool use system prompt](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview#pricing) that applies whenever any tool is present.

| Model                                               | Additional input tokens |
| --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and Claude Opus 4.7 | 325 tokens              |
| Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and earlier     | 244 tokens              |

Additional tokens are consumed by:

* Command outputs (stdout/stderr)
* Error messages
* Large file contents

See [tool use pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#tool-use-pricing) for complete pricing details.

#### Code execution tool

**Code execution is free when used with web search or web fetch.** When `web_search_20260209` (or later) or `web_fetch_20260209` (or later) is included in your API request, there are no additional charges for code execution tool calls beyond the standard input and output token costs.

When used without these tools, code execution is billed by execution time, tracked separately from token usage:

* Execution time has a minimum of 5 minutes
* Each organization receives **1,550 free hours** of usage per month
* Additional usage beyond 1,550 hours is billed at **$0.05 USD per hour, per container**
* If files are included in the request, execution time is billed even if the tool is not called, because files are preloaded onto the container

Code execution usage is tracked in the response:

```json
{
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 105,
    "output_tokens": 239,
    "server_tool_use": {
      "code_execution_requests": 1
    }
  }
}
```

#### Text editor tool

The text editor tool uses the same pricing structure as other tools used with Claude. It follows the standard input and output token pricing based on the Claude model you're using.

In addition to the base tokens, the following additional input tokens are needed for the text editor tool:

| Tool                                | Additional input tokens |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `text_editor_20250429` (Claude 4.x) | 700 tokens              |

See [tool use pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#tool-use-pricing) for complete pricing details.

#### Web search tool

Web search usage is charged in addition to token usage:

```json
{
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 105,
    "output_tokens": 6039,
    "cache_read_input_tokens": 7123,
    "cache_creation_input_tokens": 7345,
    "server_tool_use": {
      "web_search_requests": 1
    }
  }
}
```

Web search is available on the Claude API for **$10 per 1,000 searches**, plus standard token costs for search-generated content. Web search results retrieved throughout a conversation are counted as input tokens, in search iterations executed during a single turn and in subsequent conversation turns.

Each web search counts as one use, regardless of the number of results returned. If an error occurs during web search, the web search will not be billed.

#### Web fetch tool

Web fetch usage has **no additional charges** beyond standard token costs:

```json
{
  "usage": {
    "input_tokens": 25039,
    "output_tokens": 931,
    "cache_read_input_tokens": 0,
    "cache_creation_input_tokens": 0,
    "server_tool_use": {
      "web_fetch_requests": 1
    }
  }
}
```

The web fetch tool is available on the Claude API at **no additional cost**. You only pay standard token costs for the fetched content that becomes part of your conversation context.

To protect against inadvertently fetching large content that would consume excessive tokens, use the `max_content_tokens` parameter to set appropriate limits based on your use case and budget considerations.

Example token usage for typical content:

* Average web page (10 kB): \~2,500 tokens
* Large documentation page (100 kB): \~25,000 tokens
* Research paper PDF (500 kB): \~125,000 tokens

#### Computer use tool

Computer use follows the standard [tool use pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview#pricing). When using the computer use tool:

**Toolset definition overhead:** Declaring `computer_toolset_20260801` with its default members adds about 4,500 input tokens to a request (about 4,520 on Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Opus 4.8, and about 4,590 on Claude Sonnet 5), which covers the member tool definitions and the tool use system prompt. Disabling `zoom` with `configs` removes about 410 of those tokens. The exact count for a request is reported in the response `usage`, and you can estimate it in advance with the [token counting endpoint](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting).

**Earlier tool versions:** The following figures apply to the `computer_20251124` and `computer_20250124` tool versions, not to `computer_toolset_20260801`:

* System prompt overhead: 466–499 tokens added to the system prompt
* Tool definition: about 735 input tokens per tool definition (measured with `computer_20250124`)

**Additional token consumption:**

* Screenshot and zoom images returned in tool results, billed as image input (see [Vision pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision#evaluate-image-size))
* Tool execution results returned to Claude

<Note>
  If you're also using bash or text editor tools alongside computer use, those tools have their own token costs as documented in their respective pages.
</Note>

#### Browser use tool

Browser use follows the standard [tool use pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview#pricing). When using the browser use tool:

**Toolset definition overhead:** Declaring `browser_toolset_20260801` with its default members adds about 6,600 input tokens to a request (about 6,610 on Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Opus 4.8, and about 6,670 on Claude Sonnet 5), which covers the member tool definitions and the tool use system prompt. Enabling all four optional members adds about 880 tokens, and disabling members with `configs` reduces the count. The exact count for a request is reported in the response `usage`, and you can estimate it in advance with the [token counting endpoint](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/token-counting).

**Additional token consumption:**

* Screenshot and zoom images returned in tool results, billed as image input (see [Vision pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision#evaluate-image-size))
* Text tool results returned to Claude, such as accessibility trees, page text, and console or network entries

<Note>
  If you also use the computer use tool, bash tool, text editor tool, or your own tools alongside browser use, those tools have their own token costs as documented on their respective pages.
</Note>

## Claude Managed Agents pricing

[Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview) is billed on two dimensions: tokens and session runtime.

### Tokens

All tokens consumed by a Claude Managed Agents session are billed at the rates shown in [Model pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#model-pricing). [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#prompt-caching) multipliers apply identically. Web search triggered inside a session incurs the standard $10 per 1,000 searches. On [Claude Platform on AWS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#claude-platform-on-aws-pricing), session token and runtime charges convert to Claude Consumption Units at the standard rate. [Fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#fast-mode-pricing) premium pricing applies when an agent's `model.speed` is set to `"fast"`.

The [data residency multiplier](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#data-residency-pricing) also applies: when an agent's `model.inference_geo` is pinned to `"us"`, tokens consumed by sessions running that agent are billed at 1.1x the standard rates, the same multiplier that applies to US-only inference on the Messages API.

The following Messages API modifiers do **not** apply to Claude Managed Agents sessions:

| Modifier                                                                                                  | Why it doesn't apply                                           |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Batch API discount](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#batch-processing)           | Sessions are stateful and interactive. There is no batch mode. |
| [Cloud platform pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#cloud-platform-pricing) | Not available on partner-operated cloud platforms.             |

### Session runtime

| SKU             | Rate                   | Metering                  |
| --------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Session runtime | $0.08 per session-hour | `running` status duration |

Runtime is measured to the millisecond and accrues only while the session's status is `running`. Time spent `idle` (waiting for your next message or a tool confirmation), `rescheduling`, or `terminated` does not count toward runtime.

<Note>
  Session runtime replaces the [code execution](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#code-execution-tool) container-hour billing model when using Claude Managed Agents. You are not separately billed for container hours on top of session runtime.
</Note>

### Worked example

A one-hour coding session using Claude Opus 5 that consumes 50,000 input tokens and 15,000 output tokens:

| Line item       | Calculation              | Cost       |
| --------------- | ------------------------ | ---------- |
| Input tokens    | 50,000 × $5 / 1,000,000  | $0.25      |
| Output tokens   | 15,000 × $25 / 1,000,000 | $0.375     |
| Session runtime | 1.0 hour × $0.08         | $0.08      |
| **Total**       |                          | **$0.705** |

If prompt caching is active and 40,000 of the input tokens are cache reads:

| Line item             | Calculation                   | Cost       |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------- |
| Uncached input tokens | 10,000 × $5 / 1,000,000       | $0.05      |
| Cache read tokens     | 40,000 × $5 × 0.1 / 1,000,000 | $0.02      |
| Output tokens         | 15,000 × $25 / 1,000,000      | $0.375     |
| Session runtime       | 1.0 hour × $0.08              | $0.08      |
| **Total**             |                               | **$0.525** |

<Note>
  Example calculation for processing 10,000 support tickets:

  * Average \~3,700 tokens per conversation
  * Using Claude Haiku 4.5 at $1/MTok input, $5/MTok output
  * Total cost: \~$37.00 per 10,000 tickets
</Note>

For a detailed walkthrough of this calculation, see the [customer support agent guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/use-case-guides/customer-support-chat).

## Additional pricing considerations

### Cost optimization strategies

When building agents with Claude:

1. **Use appropriate models:** Choose Haiku for simple tasks, Sonnet for most production workloads, and Opus for the most complex reasoning
2. **Implement prompt caching:** Reduce costs for repeated context
3. **Batch operations:** Use the Batch API for non-time-sensitive tasks
4. **Monitor usage patterns:** Track token consumption to identify optimization opportunities

<Tip>
  For high-volume agent applications, contact the [enterprise sales team](https://claude.com/contact-sales) for custom pricing arrangements.
</Tip>

### Rate limits

Rate limits vary by usage tier and affect how many requests you can make:

* **Start tier:** Entry-level limits for getting started
* **Build tier:** Increased limits for growing applications
* **Scale tier:** Highest standard limits for production workloads

For detailed rate limit information, see [Rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits).

For limits beyond the Scale tier or custom pricing arrangements, [contact the sales team](https://claude.com/contact-sales).

### Volume discounts

Volume discounts may be available for high-volume users. These are negotiated on a case-by-case basis.

* Standard usage tiers use the pricing shown in [Model pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#model-pricing)
* Enterprise customers can [contact sales](mailto:sales@anthropic.com) for custom pricing
* Academic and research discounts may be available

### Enterprise pricing

For enterprise customers with specific needs:

* Custom rate limits
* Volume discounts
* Dedicated support
* Custom terms

Contact the sales team at [sales@anthropic.com](mailto:sales@anthropic.com) or through the [Claude Console](https://platform.claude.com/settings/limits) to discuss enterprise pricing options.

## Billing and payment

* Billing is based on actual monthly usage
* All payments are in USD
* Credit card and invoicing options available
* Usage tracking available in the [Claude Console](https://platform.claude.com/)

## Frequently asked questions

### How is token usage calculated?

Tokens are pieces of text that models process. As a rough estimate, 1 token is approximately 4 characters or 0.75 words in English. The exact count varies by language and content type.

### Are there free tiers or trials?

New users receive a small amount of free credits to test the API. [Contact sales](mailto:sales@anthropic.com) for information about extended trials for enterprise evaluation.

### How do discounts stack?

Batch API and prompt caching discounts can be combined. For example, using both features together provides significant cost savings compared to standard API calls. See [prompt caching pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing#prompt-caching) for how the multipliers interact.

### What payment methods are accepted?

Major credit cards are accepted for standard accounts. Enterprise customers can arrange invoicing and other payment methods.

For additional questions about pricing, contact [support@anthropic.com](mailto:support@anthropic.com).
